attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click on each asset to notice their names and what type of asset they are?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What images, tiles, and tilemaps do you notice in My Assets?

❓ What might each asset be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja notices the names of each of the assets on the left side of the screen, prompt them to consider how the asset might be used in the project, based on its name. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to click on each tilemap to notice how the different tile assets are used in the tilemap and which tiles have their walls turned on.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the assets in My Assets. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images, tiles, and tilemap stored in My Assets. Click on each asset to view its name, then think about what it might be used for in this project. Click on the tilemap to see where each tile is used and which tiles have their walls turned on.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use // to add comments to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming assets, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments.
steps.instructions:
Add code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add comments for: project set up, sprite set up, exit tile set up, and obstacle tile set up.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, and the asset type, followed by the name of the asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap be typed in the setCurrentTilemap function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``.
steps.instructions:
Display a tilemap on screen!


Open Scene and drag [set tilemap to (tilemap)] underneath // project set up. 


To access the tilemap created in My Assets, type assets and a dot operator before tilemap`` inside the parentheses of the setCurrentTilemap function. Then type the name given to the tilemap asset inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the documentation for help with creating a Player sprite, setting its scale, and moving the sprite around the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where can you find the coordinates of a specific tile in the tilemap editor?

❓ Why is the cameraFollowSprite function needed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Explain that coordinates begin at 0 and increase from left to right (column) and top to bottom (row). The ninja can use their cursor to hover over a specific tile, then find its coordinates in the bottom left corner of the tilemap editor.

💡 Remind the ninja that because the tilemap is larger than the size of the screen, the cameraFollowSprite function is needed to see the sprite’s movement around the screen.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding a sprite, changing its scale, and/or moving with direction buttons.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project to explore the tilemap!


Add code to create a Player sprite underneath // sprite set up. Set the sprite’s image to the sprite image asset from My Assets.


Open Scene and drag [place mySprite on top of (loc)] underneath the Player sprite’s code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. Update the tilemap coordinates in the location parameter to place the Player sprite in the top left corner of the tilemap. 


Set the Player sprite’s scale to 0.9 so that the Player sprite appears slightly smaller on screen. Then, add code to move the Player sprite around the tilemap with direction buttons. 


Then, open Scene and drag [camera follow sprite (mySprite)] underneath. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. 


Click ▶ to test the Player sprite’s code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the correct tile asset name in the getTilesbyType function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code is needed to declare an array?

❓ How is the getTilesByType function used?

❓ What code should be used to set the wall tile as the tile argument in getTilesByType?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that to declare a new array, they need to use the keyword let, the name of the array, and an assignment operator. Because the elements of the array will be generated by the getTilesByType function, they do not need to include any brackets [ ].

💡 The getTilesByType function generates an array of all the tile locations that match the image in the tile parameter. This can be useful for selecting a random tile of a certain kind or performing an action of every tile of a certain kind.

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``.
steps.instructions:
Store the values of all the wall tile locations in an array!


Underneath // exit tile set up, declare a wallTileList array to store all the wall tile locations. Open Scene and drag [array of all (tile) locations] to the right of the assignment operator. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

 tiles.getTilesByType(img` `) 

The getTilesByType function takes 1 parameter: tile. Inside the function’s parentheses, replace img` ` by typing assets, a dot operator and tile, then typing the name given to the wall tile asset inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Now, all of the wall tile locations will be stored in the wallTileList array.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the randint function to randomly select an index from a range of 0 and the length of the wallTileList array minus 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What value is stored in the randomWallTile variable?

❓ Why should a random index be selected between 0 and the length of the wallTileList array minus 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 A random index from the wallTileList array is stored in the randomWallTile variable. Because each index consists of a wall tile location, the index selected represents the random wall tile location. 

💡 Remind the ninja that arrays begin counting element indexes at 0. As a result, the length of the array is 1 larger than the last element’s index. 1 needs to be subtracted from the length of the array so that the random integer selected will be an actual index in the wallTileList array.
steps.instructions:
Select a random wall tile location from the array!


Below the wallTileList array, declare a new variable called randomWallTile. To the right of the assignment operator, type wallTileList followed by a pair of brackets [ ]. 


Select a random index from the wallTileList array using a randint function between the brackets. Keep the minimum parameter set to 0. In the max parameter, type wallTileList followed by a dot operator, then select length. Type - 1 after length, to use the index of the last element in the array as the maximum possible value. 


Now, each time the project starts, a random wall tile will be selected and stored in the randomWallTile variable.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the randomWallTile variable’s column and row values as the location parameter of getTileLocation inside the setTileAt function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will the exit tile be placed on the tilemap? How do you know?

❓ How is the setTileAt function being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The randomWallTile variable stores a random index from the wallTileList array. Each element in the array contains a wall tile’s column and row coordinates on the tilemap. The setTileAt function will use the randomWallTile variable’s coordinates to place the exit tile in its location on the tilemap. 

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Prompt them to check that they’ve selected the correct coordinate in each parameter.
steps.instructions:
Place an exit tile at the location of the random wall tile selected!


Open Scene and drag [set (tile) at (loc)] underneath // exit tile set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


tiles.setTileAt(tiles.getTileLocation(0, 0), img` `)


The setTileAt function takes 2 parameters: location and tile. Replace 0 in the col parameter by typing randomWallTile and a dot operator, then selecting column. Repeat this process in the row parameter, selecting row instead. Set the tile parameter to the exit tile asset saved in My Assets. Now, the exit tile will be set on the coordinates of a random wall tile.


Click ▶ to test that the exit tile appears on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the randomWallTile variable’s column and row values as the location parameter of getTileLocation inside the setTileAt function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will a wall be turned off in the tilemap? How do you know?

❓ How is the setWallAt function being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The randomWallTile variable stores a random index from the wallTileList array. Each element in the array contains a wall tile’s column and row coordinates on the tilemap. The setWallAt function will use the randomWallTile variable’s coordinates to turn a wall on in its location on the tilemap. This will be the same location as the exit tile.

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Prompt them to check that they’ve selected the correct coordinate in each parameter.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The exit tile still has its wall turned on, so the Player sprite can’t overlap it.


Open Scene again and drag [set wall (on) at (loc)] below the setTileAt function. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


tiles.setWallAt(tiles.getTileLocation(0, 0), false) 


The setWallAt function takes 2 parameters: location and on. Notice how the setWallAt function uses the same code in the location parameter as the setTileAt function. Set the location parameter to the randomWallTile column and row. Keep the on parameter set to false, so that the wall is turned off when the exit tile appears.


Click ▶ to test if the exit tile’s wall turns off!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the correct tile as the tile parameter of the onOverlapTile event?
steps.instructions:
Reset the project when the Player sprite overlaps the exit tile!


Open Scene and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (tile) at (location)] below // exit tile set up. Keep the kind parameter set to Player, then set the tile parameter to the exit tile asset saved in My Assets. 


Inside the onOverlapTile event’s curly brackets { } add code to reset the game.


Click ▶ to test the overlap code!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create the floorTileList array and getRandomFloor variable inside the onUpdateInterval loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code is needed to declare an array?

❓ Why should a random index be selected between 0 and the length of the floorTileList array minus 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that to declare a new array, they need to use the keyword let, the name of the array, and an assignment operator. Because the elements of the floorTileList array will be generated by the getTilesByType function, they do not need to include any brackets [ ].

💡 A random index from the floorTileList array is stored in the getRandomFloor variable. Because each element consists of a floor tile location, the index selected represents the random floor tile location. 

💡 Remind the ninja that arrays begin counting element indexes at 0. As a result, the length of the array is 1 larger than the last element’s index. 1 needs to be subtracted from the length of the array so that the random integer selected will be an actual index in the floorTileList array.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more challenging by coding obstacle tiles to appear randomly around the tilemap!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] underneath // obstacle tile set up. 


Declare a floorTileList array to store the floor tiles inside the onUpdateInterval function. Open Scene and drag [array of all (tile) locations] to the right of the assignment operator. Inside the function’s parentheses, replace img` ` by typing assets, a dot operator and tile, then typing the name given to the floor tile asset inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Below the floorTileList array, declare a new variable called getRandomFloor. To the right of the assignment operator, type floorTileList followed by a pair of brackets [ ]. Select a random index from the floorTileList array by adding a randint function between the brackets. Set the max parameter to the length of the floorTileList array minus 1. 


Now, each time the project updates, a random floor tile will be selected and stored in the getRandomFloor variable.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the getRandomFloor variable’s column and row values as the location parameter of getTileLocation inside the setTileAt function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will obstacle tiles be placed on the tilemap? How often should they appear?

❓ How is the setTileAt function being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getRandomFloor variable stores a random index from the floorTileList array. Each element in the array contains a floor tile’s column and row coordinates on the tilemap. The setTileAt function will use the getRandomFloor variable’s coordinates to place an obstacle tile in its location on the tilemap. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the parameter in the onUpdateInterval function to adjust how frequently obstacle tiles appear on the tilemap.

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Prompt the ninja to check that they’ve selected the correct coordinate in each parameter.
steps.instructions:
Set an obstacle tile to appear at the randomly selected floor tile!


Open Scene and drag [set (tile) at (loc)] inside the onUpdateInterval function. Use the getRandomFloor variable and a dot operator to set the location parameter to the column and row location of the random floor tile selected. Set the tile parameter to the obstacle tile asset saved in My Assets. Now, the obstacle tile will be set on the coordinates of a random floor tile.


Click ▶ to see the obstacle tiles appear on random floor tiles around the tilemap! Tinker with the parameter in the onUpdateInterval function to make the obstacle tiles appear more or less frequently.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the getRandomFloor variable’s column and row values as the location parameter of getTileLocation inside the setTileAt function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the obstacle tile appear in the same location that a wall is turned on? 

❓ How is the setWallAt function being used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getRandomFloor variable stores a random index from the floorTileList array. Each element in the array contains a floor tile’s column and row coordinates on the tilemap. The setWallAt function will use the getRandomFloor variable’s coordinates to turn a wall on in its location on the tilemap. 

💡 A wall should be turned on at the location of an obstacle tile so that there is a visual cue for the user and so that they can avoid the obstacles as they appear on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite is able to move through the obstacle tiles!


Open Scene again and drag [set wall (on) at (loc)]  inside the onUpdateInterval function. Set the location parameter to the getRandomFloor column and row. Change the on parameter to true, so that the wall is turned on wherever the obstacle tile appears.


Click ▶ to test  if the obstacle tiles’ walls turn on!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use .length to check if the number of items in the floor tile array was equal to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will cause the number of floor tiles on the tilemap to decrease? 

❓ What will happen if there are no more floor tiles on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that each time an obstacle tile is created, the number of floor tiles decreases by 1. There will be no floor tiles left once the obstacle tiles populate the entire tilemap. This will cause the game to end in a loss. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to review their if conditional to make sure they have used the correct syntax and tile asset in the getTilesByType function.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
Add a lose condition when there are no more floor tiles!


Drag an if conditional inside the onUpdateInterval function. Delete true, then open Scene and drag [array of all (tile) locations] inside the parentheses. Set the tile parameter to the floor tile saved in My Assets. 


Then, type a dot operator and select length. Type an equality operator == followed by 0, then add code to make the game end in a loss when the length of the floor tile array is 0.


Click ▶ to test the game over condition!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the changeScoreBy function inside the onHitWall event so that the score decreases any time the Player sprite bumps into a wall tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the Player sprite bumps into a wall?

❓ How many points might the Player sprite start the project with? How much should they decrease by, on overlap with a wall?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Each time the Player sprite bumps into a wall, the score will decrease. The onHitWall event can be useful for making something happen each time a sprite bumps into multiple types of tiles (e.g. tiles with different images, that all have walls turned on). 

💡 Prompt the ninja to try out different values in the setScore and changeScoreBy functions to find an engaging combination for the project.
steps.instructions:
Change the score when the Player sprite bumps into a wall tile!


Add code to set the score underneath // project set up. Set the value argument to a large positive number, such as 1000.


Open Scene and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) hits wall at (location)] underneath // obstacle tile set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

scene.onHitWall(SpriteKind.Player, function(sprite: Sprite, location: tiles.Location) { }) 

The onHitWall function takes 2 parameters: kind and handler. Use the default values for each parameter.


Add code to change the score inside the onHitWall event. Set the value argument to -1, so that the score decreases each time the Player sprite bumps into a wall.


Click ▶ to test the score code. Tinker with the values to increase or decrease the challenge of the game!

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the if condition so the project checks if the score is less than 0?
steps.instructions:
Add another lose condition to end the project when the score reaches 0!


Drag an if conditional inside the onHitWall event. Replace true with code that checks if the score is less than or equal to 0, then ends the game in a loss.


Click ▶ to test out this game over condition!

subgroups.title: Avoid the Haystacks!
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses tilemap overlap events to make something happen when a sprite overlaps different types of wall tiles!

validationItems.text: Display a tilemap asset on screen.
Create a Player sprite using an image asset, place the sprite on a specific tilemap location, and set the camera to follow it.
Create wallTileList and floorTileList arrays to store the wall tile and floor tile locations.
Create randomWallTile and getRandomFloor variables to select a random index from the wall and floor tile arrays.
Set an exit tile and turn the wall off at the tilemap location of the random wall tile selected.
Reset the game when the Player sprite overlaps the exit tile.
Set an obstacle tile and turn a wall on at the random floor tile location selected.
End the game if there are 0 floor tiles on the tilemap.
Decrease the score when the Player sprite bumps into a wall.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about tilemap overlap events and how to make different things happen when sprites overlap different tiles and walls. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: The Big Event
badges.description: Use events to control what happens to sprites navigating a tilemap in a project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Touch Controls
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite overlaps a specific tile.

badges.title: A Chain of Reactions
badges.description: Make something happen when a sprite hits a wall.

badges.title: A Glyph in the System
badges.description: Use an image asset as a cursor image in a dialog box.

badges.title: Save for Later
badges.description: Create an array to store all of the locations of a specific tile type on a tilemap.

badges.title: Invisible Walls
badges.description: Turn a wall on or off at a specific location on a tilemap.
